summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record; the operative rules for a visitor in the department are the national laws and enforcement patterns recorded below.

The most direct legal exposure concerns public restrooms. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banning 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote; its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for the narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, states that the provision directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and argues that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement reaches private life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom restriction's practical burden falls on whoever controls access: LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that compliance would rest on security staff's personal judgment, including demands for identification, which raises the odds of being challenged or outed at a venue entrance in Apurímac as anywhere else in Peru.

Peru's hate-violence record is comparatively severe within South America. The country is one of only three on the continent, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, and the 2020-2023 homicide tally of 54 TLGBI people shows the gap between statute and street.

Recorded figures understate the problem. Gianna Camacho describes the published data as a sub-registry, and the 170 rights-violation cases logged over 2020-2023 include state violence as well as private attacks, so official counts should be read as a floor rather than a measure of exposure.

Regional comparison: the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 binds Peru to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy, and the Azul Rojas Marín judgment shows that litigation through the Inter-American Commission can still produce a conviction where domestic enforcement fails.
localsOnly:
Residents of Apurímac live under the same national statutes as visitors, but the enforcement burden is heavier for those without the means to travel or litigate: the Azul Rojas Marín case took nearly 20 years and years of litigation to reach a sentence, and the December 2025 conviction of officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León was Peru's first in a case motivated by sexual discrimination.

Healthcare access improved on paper in June 2024, when Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance; how far that guidance has reached facilities in Apurímac is not sourced here.

The April 2025 law's article 4 ban on media and advertising content, together with the rise in the minimum obscenity sentence from three to four years, constrains local publishers, artists and educators, not only visitors.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist legal challenge, a remedy available to Apurímac residents through the same national courts.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record; whether the department's municipal authorities have issued their own signage or facility rules is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the April 2025 restroom provision has been enforced by security staff, police or municipal inspectors anywhere in Apurímac is unresolved; the only documented enforcement action in the inventory is a national consumer-protection body's dismissal of a trans woman's complaint against a gym.

The bills reached committee stage as of February 2025 and were approved by the Plenary on 2 April 2025; whether the merged text has since been challenged before the Constitutional Court, and with what outcome, is unresolved on this record.

Whether the June 2024 health-guidance revision has been implemented at health facilities in Apurímac, and whether the department recorded any of the 54 homicides or 170 rights-violation cases logged nationally over 2020-2023, is not sourced here.
